tagline.text: A Spanish colonial city of cobblestone streets echoing with carriage bells

children.text: A trading city founded by Spain in the 16th century, recognized as Asia's most intact Spanish colonial townscape and inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The cobblestones of Calle Crisologo, kalesa carriages, and Ilocos empanada welcome travelers.

Vigan, the capital of Ilocos Sur in northwestern Luzon, is a historic city sitting at the mouth of the Mestizo River near the South China Sea. After the Spanish conquistador Juan de Salcedo established a base here in

, Vigan flourished as northern Luzon's outpost in the galleon trade network linking Chinese merchants from Fujian with Acapulco, Mexico. The mansions built by the Chinese-mestizo merchant families who grew wealthy from this trade form today's old town.

Vigan's mansions follow a distinctive style called "bahay na bato" (house of stone). The ground floor is built thick with brick and lime, used for storerooms and shops, while the second floor is built of wood with capiz-shell windows and used as living space. Blending Chinese brickwork, Spanish urban planning, and a structure suited to the Philippine tropical climate, UNESCO inscribed Vigan as a World Heritage Site in
as "the best-preserved planned Spanish colonial town in Asia."

Unlike Manila's Intramuros, which was largely destroyed during World War II, Vigan escaped major damage in the war, leaving its old streets almost intact. It was also named one of the "New7Wonders Cities" in
. After sunset, gaslamp-style streetlights illuminate the cobblestones, and the sight of kalesa (horse-drawn carriages) passing by feels as if time has stopped.

Vigan is ideal for travelers who love history, architecture, photography, and food, and being a small, walkable city, it works fine for family trips too. Combining it with Laoag and Paoay makes it easy to expand into a loop around the Ilocos region.

Vigan's iconic cobblestone street, lined on both sides with two-story mansions and closed to most vehicle traffic. Enjoy the souvenir shops and cafes by day and the illuminated street atmosphere by night. It's worth walking the same street twice, once in daylight and once at night.
A tour of the city's sights by horse-drawn carriage. There's an hourly rate (about
for
1 hour
) or a fixed rate for a sightseeing loop, so settle the route and fare before you set off.

blocks.title: St. Paul's Cathedral and the Plaza Salcedo fountain show

children.text: The cathedral, built in "Earthquake Baroque" style with thick walls to withstand tremors, and the plaza in front of it form the heart of Vigan. Every evening, a fountain show set to music takes place at the pond in Plaza Salcedo.

blocks.title: Syquia Mansion and the Crisologo Museum

children.text: At the Syquia family mansion, connected to the sixth Philippine president Elpidio Quirino, and the former Crisologo family home turned into a museum, you can see how the upper class lived in that era.
A workshop making the traditional Ilocos jars called "burnay." You can watch the potter's wheel shape clay and try your hand at it yourself.
The bell tower of Bantay Church, about
5–10 minutes
from downtown by tricycle, offers a hilltop view over the whole Vigan area. In the past it also served as a watchtower for spotting pirate raids.
Baluarte, a privately run free zoo, and Hidden Garden, a garden with tropical plants and a cafe, are both popular with families.

This orange-colored fried empanada, made from a rice-flour dough filled with shredded green papaya, egg, and Vigan longganisa, is a must on any Vigan trip. Try one dipped in vinegar sauce from a stall at Plaza Burgos.

on a regular air-conditioned bus. Taking an overnight bus gets you there early in the morning, letting you make the most of the day.
Deluxe buses with more legroom cost more, but are more comfortable for the long ride.

The old town is easily explored on foot. For sights a little further out, use a tricycle (about
for a short trip in town) or a kalesa.
Vehicle access to Calle Crisologo is restricted, so if your accommodation is on the street itself, you may need to carry your luggage in on foot from the entrance.
The Ilocos region has a clear dry and wet season. In the dry season,
November–May
, rain is rare and walking is pleasant, and
December–February
is relatively cool, good even for midday walking tours.
March–May
is very hot and dry, with midday temperatures sometimes topping
, so plan your schedule around mornings and evenings.
June–October
is the rainy season, affected by the southwest monsoon and typhoons, and northwestern Luzon gets especially heavy rainfall in
July–September
. Notable festivals include the Vigan Longganisa Festival around the city's founding anniversary on
January 22
, and the Viva Vigan Arts Festival in
early May
, filled with street performances and traditional costume parades. Old town accommodation sells out early during Holy Week and year-end, so book ahead.

In Vigan, it's well worth staying at least once in a heritage hotel converted from an old mansion. Calle Crisologo and the surrounding lanes have several centuries-old bahay na bato mansions turned into hotels, impressive for their high ceilings, wooden floors, and antique furniture. Prices run about
per night. If your budget is smaller, a guesthouse on the edge of the old town (about
) works fine too — just pick a spot you can walk to Calle Crisologo from.

Vigan is also one of the Philippines' foremost food cities. Signature dishes include the strongly garlicky, tangy Vigan longganisa, crispy fried pork belly bagnet, the tangy beef-innard soup sinanglao, shrimp fritters okoy, and the Ilocano vegetable stew pinakbet. "Cafe Leona," an old restaurant at the end of Calle Crisologo, has been a landmark for a long time, and the empanada stalls at Plaza Burgos get crowded with locals every evening. Good gifts include Vigan longganisa, the Ilocos vinegar "sukang Iloco," and traditional abel textiles.
For photos of Calle Crisologo, shoot around
6–7 AM
, when it's nearly empty and you can frame just the cobblestones and mansions.
When taking a kalesa, agree clearly beforehand on whether the fare is per "
1 hour
" or per "route." It's best to avoid a driver who appears to mistreat the horse.
The midday sun is very strong. Bring a parasol or hat and water, and rest at a museum or cafe during the hottest hours.
Downtown Vigan has plenty of ATMs and convenience stores, but street stalls and kalesa only accept cash.
The fountain show usually runs several times each evening, but the schedule and whether it runs at all can change, so check locally.
Souvenirs tend to be a bit cheaper at shops one block away from Calle Crisologo.
If you're flying through Laoag Airport, consider combining the trip with Ilocos Norte sights such as Paoay Church (a World Heritage site) and Batac Church.
Calle Crisologo's cobblestones are uneven and slippery when wet. Avoid high heels, and watch your footing at night.
Don't touch the antique furniture and artifacts inside the mansions and museums, and follow any no-photography signs.
Watch out for pickpockets during crowded evening hours and festival periods.
Midday walking tours in
March–May
carry a risk of heatstroke. Drink plenty of water.
Don't agree to touts' "special tours" or excessive kalesa fares, and check the price first.
During the rainy season and typhoon season, the northern coastal road can flood or buses can be delayed.
